DecisionBench: A Benchmark for Emergent Delegation in Long-Horizon Agentic Workflows

Yuxuan Gao Affiliation: OpenMesh AI    Megan Wang Affiliation: OpenMesh AI    Yi Ling Yu Affiliation: OpenMesh AI    Zijian Carl Ma Affiliation: Stanford University    Ao Qu Affiliation: MIT∗* Equal contribution (alphabetical order)Code and data:https://huggingface.co/decisionbench Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Affiliation: Columbia University
Abstract

We introduce DecisionBench, a benchmark substrate for emergent delegation in long-horizon agentic workflows. The substrate fixes a task suite (GAIA, τ\tau-bench, BFCL multi-turn), a peer-model pool (11 models, 7 vendor families), a delegation interface (call_model plus an optional read_profile channel), a deterministic skill-annotation layer, and a multi-axis metric suite covering quality, cost, latency, delegation rate, routing fidelity-at-kk, vendor self-preference, and a counterfactual-delegation ceiling. The substrate is agnostic to how peer information is generated or delivered, so learned routers, richer peer memories, adaptive profile construction, and multi-step delegation can all be evaluated against it. We characterize the substrate with a five-condition reference sweep on the full pool (n=23,375n{=}23{,}375 task instances). Three benchmark-level findings emerge: (i) mean end-task quality is statistically indistinguishable across the four awareness conditions (|β|≤0.010|\beta|{\leq}0.010, p≥0.21p{\geq}0.21), so quality-only evaluation would miss the orchestration signal; (ii) routing fidelity-at-11 ranges from 7.5%7.5\% to 29.5%29.5\% across conditions at near-equal mean quality, with delivery channel (on-demand tool vs. preloaded description) dominating description content; (iii) a counterfactual ceiling places perfect delegation 1515–3131 percentage points above measured performance on every suite, locating large unrealized headroom for future orchestration methods. We release the substrate, annotation layer, reference intervention suite, analysis pipeline, and 220 per-condition run archives.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed for tasks that span minutes to hours of tool use [49, 44], with the dominant cost shifting from per-token quality to compute spent on sub-tasks where a smaller or differently-specialized peer model would have sufficed [24, 6, 13]. Routing a sub-task to a peer rather than solving it locally is therefore a Pareto-frontier shifter alongside raw model capability. A practitioner deploying an agentic system today must decide whether to delegate, to whom, and what (if anything) to tell the orchestrator about its peers. These decisions are typically made by intuition because no benchmark has measured them in isolation.

Existing agentic benchmarks measure single-agent capability on a fixed task — GAIA [23], τ\tau-bench [47], BFCL [29] and others (§2). Multi-agent systems work [43, 11] typically uses hand-coded role assignment rather than emergent delegation. Cost-aware routing benchmarks [24, 13] treat routing as a learned external policy rather than a behavior the orchestrator must exhibit on its own. SkillsBench [17] measures skill scaffolds attached to a single agent. None of these directly measure whether an agent delegates well between peer models in the course of solving a long-horizon task, or what process-level metrics would reveal about how those delegation decisions are made.

We introduce DecisionBench, a benchmark substrate for emergent delegation in long-horizon agentic workflows. The substrate fixes (1) a task suite (GAIA, τ\tau-bench, BFCL multi-turn, with deterministic Stage-1/Stage-2 splits), (2) a peer-model pool (11 models from 7 vendor families pinned to a freeze date), (3) a delegation interface (a call_model tool, optionally paired with a read_profile channel for peer-information interventions), (4) an annotation layer (a frozen 7-skill taxonomy and a deterministic step tagger, released as evaluation machinery rather than a method we propose), and (5) a metric suite covering end-task quality, cost, latency, delegation rate, routing fidelity-at-kk, vendor self-preference, and a counterfactual-delegation ceiling. The substrate is agnostic to how peer information is generated or delivered; methods that produce learned routers, richer peer memories, adaptive profile construction, or multi-step delegation can all be evaluated against it.

To demonstrate how DecisionBench evaluates peer-awareness interventions, we instantiate four reference conditions over the released annotation layer, against a no-information baseline: (blind) only call_model, no peer description; (aware-c1/c2/c3) preload a peer description constructed three different ways — a curated rubric, deterministic statistics from Stage-1 traces, or dual out-of-pool LLM-judge summaries — and expose read_profile; and (aware-tool-only) the same tools as the aware variants but with the preloaded description suppressed, a one-variable ablation that isolates delivery channel from description content. These reference interventions are not part of the benchmark definition; they are the baselines we use to demonstrate the substrate and to seed comparisons for future methods.

Findings.

Across the 5-condition reference sweep on the 11-model pool (11×3×5=16511{\times}3{\times}5{=}165 cells, n=23,375n{=}23{,}375 tasks), three benchmark-level patterns emerge. (1) End-task quality is mostly flat across awareness conditions (|β|≤0.010|\beta|{\leq}0.010, p≥0.21p{\geq}0.21 in a mixed-effects fit), so quality-only evaluation would miss the orchestration signal entirely. (2) Delegation fidelity moves cleanly: on-demand tool access (aware-tool-only) more than doubles routing precision-at-11 over blind (14.2%→29.5%14.2\%{\to}29.5\%) at quality parity and lower mean cost; preloaded variants capture less than half of the gain (C2 20.8%20.8\%, C3 15.5%15.5\%; C1 7.5%7.5\%, below blind). The dissociation between fidelity and quality is itself the methodological payoff of measuring process-level metrics, not just outcomes. (3) A counterfactual-delegation ceiling places perfect single-step delegation 15–31 pp above measured performance on every suite, locating substantial unrealized headroom for future orchestration methods. We additionally document cross-vendor self-preference in delegation behavior at 1.51.5–3.7×3.7\times chance.

Contributions.

(1) The DecisionBench benchmark for emergent delegation in long-horizon agentic workflows: a fixed task suite, peer-model pool, delegation interface, annotation layer (frozen 7-skill taxonomy plus deterministic step tagger), and a multi-axis metric suite (quality, cost, latency, delegation rate, fidelity-at-kk, vendor self-preference, counterfactual ceiling). (2) A reference intervention suite for peer-awareness on the benchmark: three profile-card content variants (curated rubric, deterministic statistics, dual out-of-pool LLM-judge summary) and a delivery-channel ablation (aware-tool-only) that isolates information content from delivery mechanism. These are baselines on DecisionBench, not part of the benchmark definition. (3) An empirical characterization of the substrate using the reference suite: end-task quality is statistically flat across awareness conditions, delivery channel dominates description content, and the perfect-delegation ceiling exceeds measured performance by 15–31 pp on every suite — patterns visible only through the process-level metrics the benchmark instruments. (4) Documented cross-vendor self-preference in delegation behavior, the orchestration-tool analogue of LLM-as-judge biases [52, 27, 41, 31].

2 Related Work

Agentic benchmarks.

GAIA [23] introduced a general-assistant benchmark framed against the single-shot evaluation limitation; τ\tau-bench [47] tests multi-turn state tracking under domain policy [16, 1]; SWE-Bench [14] and SWE-Bench Pro [32] cover repository-level coding; BFCL [29] and ToolLLM [30] measure function-calling correctness; WebArena [53], Mind2Web [7], and WebShop [46] cover web environments; ALFWorld [37] and OSWorld [45] cover embodied / desktop-OS settings; AgentBench [19] aggregates many; MLE-bench [5] and Cybench [50] target ML engineering and cybersecurity. We use GAIA, τ\tau-bench, and BFCL as heterogeneous quality probes spanning open-ended retrieval, dialogue, and structured tool calls.

Skill-aware agent design.

SkillsBench [17] measures the contribution of skill scaffolds to agent configurations such as Claude Code and Codex CLI; related lines extend single-agent capability through chained reasoning [42, 48, 40, 15], self-feedback [36, 22], open-ended exploration [38, 28], constitution-style behavior shaping [2, 26], and long-context processing [3, 12]. DecisionBench differs in (1) testing raw model APIs rather than product configurations and (2) treating “skill knowledge” as peer capabilities surfaced to a different agent that may delegate, letting us measure whether structured peer knowledge improves cross-model delegation — a question single-agent skill scaffolds cannot address.

Cost-aware orchestration and routing.

RouteLLM [24] and FrugalGPT [6] treat routing as a learned external policy; HybridLLM [8], AutoMix [21], EcoAssistant [51], and RouterBench [13] extend the policy line, while mixture- and society-of-agents formulations [39, 9, 35] distribute work with hand-coded coordination. DecisionBench measures emergent orchestration with no external policy and no hard-coded roles — the baseline before any router is trained.

LLM-as-judge for trace analysis.

LLM judging [52, 18] is now a standard substitute for human evaluation, with documented self-preference [27], position [41], and length [31] biases. DecisionBench’s C3 profile variant uses this technique for trace analysis (§4.2); we mitigate self-preference by using two judges from families outside the agent pool and surfacing both judgments side-by-side rather than averaging.

3 DecisionBench: Benchmark Substrate

DecisionBench is a fixed substrate for measuring emergent delegation in long-horizon agentic workflows. It comprises a task suite (§3.1), a peer-model pool (§3.2), a delegation interface (§3.3), an annotation layer (§3.4) used as evaluation machinery rather than as a proposed orchestration method, and a metric suite (§3.5). The substrate is agnostic to how peer information is generated, summarized, or delivered; the reference interventions we use to characterize it in §4 are one family of methods among many it admits.

3.1 Task suites and splits

DecisionBench draws long-horizon agentic tasks from three established benchmarks, partitioned into a Stage-1 (profiling) split and a Stage-2 (evaluation) split via a deterministic 20/80 stratified sample (seed=10): GAIA [23] (general tool-use QA, exact-match scoring; stratified by Level, 32 / 133 tasks within the validation set since the public test-set leaderboard is non-functional, see §8); τ\tau-bench [47] (tool-agent-user dialogue, passkk; stratified by sub-domain into airline / retail shards); BFCL v4 multi-turn [29] (function-calling, AST-match on per-turn calls, see §8; stratified by task family). The Stage-1 split is the basis for any profile-building intervention (§4); the Stage-2 split is the held-out evaluation set on which all reported numbers are measured. “Long-horizon” here means multi-step trajectories within a task, not multi-hour deployments. SWE-Bench Pro is excluded from headline results (Docker harness unreliable in our regime) and reported only as appendix material.

3.2 Peer-model pool

Eleven models across seven vendor families (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Qwen, MiniMax), pinned to a 2026-04-29 freeze date and routed via OpenRouter [25]. The pool is intentionally heterogeneous in vendor, size class, and reasoning-mode capability so that delegation is plausibly useful. Full per-model list in Appendix A.

3.3 Delegation interface

A DecisionBench orchestrator is an LLM agent running the Stage-2 task loop with at least one tool, call_model(name, subtask, budget_usd), that delegates a sub-task to a named peer in the pool. The peer receives only the orchestrator’s subtask string plus its own system prompt; it does not see earlier turns. The peer’s return value is the orchestrator’s tool result, after which the orchestrator continues the task. A delegation cap of 10 peer calls per task bounds runaway loops; no other constraint is imposed.

The benchmark also defines an optional second tool, read_profile(model), which returns a structured description of the named peer. This tool is the channel through which peer-information interventions are delivered to the orchestrator. A method that does not consume peer information at all (e.g., the blind baseline in §4) simply omits this tool. The benchmark does not specify what read_profile returns; that is part of the intervention being evaluated.

3.4 Annotation layer: skill taxonomy and step tagger

To enable process-level evaluation of delegation decisions — specifically, whether a delegation was sent to a peer well-suited to the sub-task — DecisionBench ships an annotation layer. The annotation layer is part of the benchmark’s analysis machinery, not a proposed orchestration method; methods are free to use it, ignore it, or replace it with their own.

A fixed 7-skill taxonomy (App. C, Table 4) is frozen prior to any tagging: tool-call schema adherence (BFCLprimary{}_{\text{primary}}); multi-turn state tracking (τ\tau); domain-policy compliance (τ\tau); information retrieval (GAIA, τ\tau); multi-step reasoning (GAIA); numerical computation (GAIA, τ\tau); long-input handling (GAIA). Each skill has at least one primary suite, so the taxonomy exercises observable behavior on every cell. A deterministic rule-based step tagger (App. D, version-pinned) assigns at most one skill to each step of an agent trajectory using trace-only signal (tool name, finish reason, input-token threshold ≥15\geq 15K, refusal-phrase regex), with no LLM judgment. The tagger is the basis for two evaluation primitives in the metric suite: per-(model, skill) Stage-1 pass-rate statistics (which define the “Stage-1-best peer for a skill” used in fidelity and ceiling metrics) and the dominant-skill assignment for each Stage-2 delegation context. An emergent-taxonomy audit (App. E) finds that 94.5%94.5\% of a free-form LLM-judge re-tagging on a sub-sample maps cleanly to one of the seven labels.

3.5 Metrics

DecisionBench reports a multi-axis profile per orchestration method, spanning outcome and process:

Quality / cost / latency. Per-suite native quality (GAIA exact match, τ\tau-bench passkk, BFCL AST match), cost in USD per task at freeze-date OpenRouter pricing, and wall-clock latency.

Quality-cost trade-off. 2D Pareto hypervolume in (q,−cost)(q,-\text{cost}) space against a fixed cost reference (×1.05\!\times max observed mean cost per benchmark), with paired-bootstrap 95% CIs (nboot=5000n_{\text{boot}}{=}5000) on the difference vs. a designated baseline condition.

Delegation rate. Mean call_model invocations per task, per (model, suite, condition).

Delegation fidelity@kk. For every observed call_model invocation, the rule-based tagger infers the dominant skill of the orchestrator’s pre-call trajectory; we rank candidate peers by their Stage-1 pass rate on that skill and report the share of delegations that pick one of the top-kk (k∈{1,3}k\in\{1,3\}). This is a process-level routing-quality signal that does not depend on the final task outcome.

Vendor self-preference. For each delegation we record the (orchestrator vendor, peer vendor) pair and compare the observed same-vendor share against the chance-level rate implied by pool composition (a vendor with kk peers in an NN-pool has expected same-vendor share (k−1)/(N−1)(k{-}1)/(N{-}1)).

Counterfactual-delegation ceiling. For each blind task we compute the most-optimistic outcome if the orchestrator had delegated the entire task to its Stage-1-best peer on the inferred dominant skill, with the peer answering at its empirical Stage-1 pass rate. This bound is an explicit upper envelope under stated assumptions (App. U) and serves as unrealized-headroom information for future methods.

Paired-bootstrap CIs throughout are matched on task id, with τ\tau-bench task ids prefixed by env shard so airline-task-0 is distinct from retail-task-0. The full per-task records (∼\sim23k rows under the reference sweep in §5) are released as records.jsonl.gz so every numerical claim is reproducible from a single analysis script.

4 Reference Awareness Conditions

The following five conditions are not part of the benchmark definition; they are reference interventions instantiated on DecisionBench to demonstrate how peer-awareness mechanisms are evaluated and to seed comparisons for future methods. Each intervention is fully specified by (i) what read_profile returns (the description content), and (ii) whether the same content is also preloaded into the orchestrator’s system prompt (the delivery channel).

A concrete profile-card instance.

To ground the construction details that follow, we first present a representative artifact: the abridged C2 card for claude-opus-4.7, rendered exactly as it would appear in the orchestrator’s context window.

---
model: claude-opus-4.7; variant: c2_static; tagger: v2.0-2026-05-01;
n_tasks: 105; benchmarks: [bfcl, gaia, tau-bench]
---
claude-opus-4.7 — derived skill profile (C2). Generated automatically from 105 Stage-1 tasks across 3 benchmarks. No LLM judgment; reproducible from trace zips alone.
Strengths. Domain-policy compliance (rank 2/10, 9/11= 82%9/11\,{=}\,82\% pass, $0.069/success); numerical computation (3/11, 27/34= 79%27/34\,{=}\,79\%, $0.163/success); tool-call schema adherence (5/11, 41/52= 79%41/52\,{=}\,79\%).
Weaknesses. Long-input handling (rank 2/8, 12/22= 55%12/22\,{=}\,55\%, $1.96/success); information retrieval (4/11, 35/46= 76%35/46\,{=}\,76\%); multi-turn state tracking (5/11, 57/73= 78%57/73\,{=}\,78\%).
All measured skills. Skill pass nn avg steps avg out-tok $/task Domain-policy 82%82\% 11 1.2 256 0.056 Information retrieval 76%76\% 46 3.7 453 0.142 Multi-turn state tracking 78%78\% 73 8.3 504 0.258 …

The C1 variant replaces the strength/weakness sentences with curated vendor-claim citations and curator notes; C3 replaces them with two judge-written prose paragraphs (Grok-4, Llama-4-Maverick) preserved side-by-side. All three variants share the ⟨\langleYAML frontmatter, strengths, weaknesses, all-skills table⟩\rangle skeleton; the full set of 11×3=3311{\times}3{=}33 cards is released under profile_cards/.

4.1 Blind delegation baseline

blind exposes only call_model with the peer-name list and no skill information; read_profile is not attached. The orchestrator delegates entirely from priors over peer names. This is the no-information reference against which the four awareness interventions below are compared. Empirically (see Table 2) blind delegation rates are 0.02 on τ\tau-bench, 0.17 on BFCL, and 0.41 on GAIA per task, so blind quality is within ∼\sim1–2 pp of solo on τ\tau-bench and BFCL and serves as the operative no-delegation baseline on those two suites; a full Stage-2 solo (no-call_model-tool) cell is queued for a future release.

4.2 Profile-card content variants

The three content variants share schema and differ only in construction; all are rendered as markdown for an agent’s context window. Per-(model, skill) Stage-1 static metrics (pass rate, mean tokens, mean steps, mean latency, cost-per-success) are the arithmetic primitive on which C2 is built, and which C3 judges read alongside raw traces.

C1 (structured-rubric anchor): a curated per-skill profile assembled from public sources only (vendor model cards, public leaderboards [33, 29, 17, 20]) with provenance markers; single-curator, pre-registered at a dated git hash, treated as a structured-rubric anchor rather than a validated human baseline.

C2 (static-metric): deterministic statistics over the agent’s own Stage-1 traces (per-(model, skill) pass rate, tokens, steps, latency, cost-per-success, percentile rank), end-to-end reproducible from released zips with tagger version pinned. No LLM judgment, so reviewer disagreement collapses to verifiable arithmetic.

C3 (dual-LLM-judge): free-form skill summaries from two out-of-pool judges (xAI Grok-4, Meta Llama-4-Maverick) that read each candidate’s Stage-1 traces independently; both judgments preserved side-by-side, not synthesized. Inter-judge Spearman ρ¯\bar{\rho} (App. Q) is itself a measurable sub-metric.

4.3 Delivery channels: preloaded versus on-demand

The same description content can reach an orchestrator through two qualitatively different channels: pasted into the system prompt before the task starts (preloaded), or retrievable through a read_profile tool call mid-task (on-demand). The aware conditions span both axes:

  • •

    aware-c1, aware-c2, aware-c3 — call_model + read_profile serving the matching C1/C2/C3 card on demand, with the same description also preloaded in the system prompt.

  • •

    aware-tool-only — same tools as aware-c2 (the C2 card is what read_profile returns), but with the preloaded peer description suppressed. This is a one-variable ablation against aware-c2, pinning content at C2 and isolating the delivery-channel axis.

Cards are served on demand so which cards the agent reads is itself measurable behavior.

4.4 Stage-2 condition summary

Table 1 summarizes the five conditions on the content×\timesdelivery axes.

5 Experimental Setup

We characterize the substrate by running the five reference conditions on the eleven-model pool, yielding 11​ models×3​ benchmarks×5​ conditions=16511\text{ models}\times 3\text{ benchmarks}\times 5\text{ conditions}=165 cells (220 run zips after τ\tau-bench airline/retail sharding). Each cell evaluates 133 GAIA tasks, 132 τ\tau-bench tasks, or 160 BFCL tasks against the substrate metric suite (§3.5); total n=23,375n{=}23{,}375 task instances. All scoring is post-hoc against the canonical metrics. Compute budget and per-model spend are detailed in App. H.

For statistical inference we use two estimators. Paired-bootstrap 95% CIs on Δ​q\Delta q vs. blind are matched on task id (nboot=5000n_{\text{boot}}{=}5000, basic / Hall-reflected). For the global test that any aware condition shifts mean quality, we fit a random-intercept mixed-effects model q∼cond+(1|agent×benchmark)q\sim\text{cond}+(1|\text{agent}\times\text{benchmark}) on the 23,37523{,}375 task rows with statsmodels [34]; the full output is in App. T. Random slopes for cond did not converge under any of four optimizers we tried, so the fit is random-intercept only; this is conservative since unmodeled task-level variance inflates residual SEs.

Released artifacts.

We release: the DecisionBench substrate (decision_bench/ task / pool / interface / metric code); the annotation layer (tagger.py v2.0, frozen 7-skill taxonomy, 200200-step emergent-audit CSV); the reference intervention suite (profile_cards/ with all 33 cards in three variants, plus the aware-tool-only ablation harness); the analysis pipeline; and 220 per-condition run archives spanning ∼\sim23,000 task-level traces. The C2 cards are reproducible from the released zips via tools/build_c2_profile.py; the C3 cards via tools/build_c3_profile.py (∼\sim$10–$20 of judge inference).

6 Results

We organize results around six questions DecisionBench is designed to answer about a peer-awareness intervention: (§6.1) does it improve mean end-task quality? (§6.2) where is the signal hidden in the aggregate, across agents and suites? (§6.3) does delivery channel or description content matter more? (§6.4) does it improve which peer the orchestrator chooses? (§6.5) what failure modes does the benchmark surface? (§6.6) how much unrealized headroom remains for future methods?

6.1 End-task quality is mostly flat across awareness conditions

Mean end-task quality is statistically indistinguishable across the four awareness conditions, on every suite. Routing fidelity, in contrast, produces a clear ordering across the same five conditions (§6.4); the dissociation is the methodological payoff of measuring process- and outcome-level metrics together. Table 2 reports per-condition aggregates; Fig. 2 shows the underlying quality–cost frontiers.

Awareness improves routing precision. Awareness lifts routing fidelity@1 in three of four conditions: blind 14.2% →\to aware-c1 7.5%, aware-c2 20.8%, aware-c3 15.5%, aware-tool-only 29.5%. On-demand tool access drives the largest gain; partial-preload C2 and C3 capture roughly half; only the rubric variant (C1) underperforms blind. Mean quality is flat across all four awareness conditions: Δ\Deltaq is {−1.2,−0.4,−1.4,+0.1}\{-1.2,-0.4,-1.4,+0.1\} pp on GAIA, {+0.1,−2.3,−0.3,−0.1}\{+0.1,-2.3,-0.3,-0.1\} pp on τ\tau-bench, and {−0.5,−0.4,−0.8,+0.3}\{-0.5,-0.4,-0.8,+0.3\} pp on BFCL for aware-c1/c2/c3/tool-only. A mixed-effects regression q∼cond+(1|agent×benchmark)q\sim\text{cond}+(1\,|\,\text{agent}\!\times\!\text{benchmark}) on 23,375 task rows confirms all four aware coefficients are indistinguishable from blind (β∈{−0.005,−0.010,−0.008,+0.001}\beta\in\{-0.005,-0.010,-0.008,+0.001\}, all p≥0.21p\geq 0.21); the largest pairwise contrast is C2 vs. tool-only Δ​β^=−0.011\Delta\hat{\beta}{=}-0.011, p=0.18p{=}0.18 (full table App. I). This dissociation — fidelity moves cleanly across conditions while mean quality does not — is itself a methodological finding: process-level metrics detect orchestration design differences that quality-only evaluation misses. Whether the routing-fidelity gain propagates to outcome at larger sample sizes or under multi-step delegation is open work (§8).

Negative Δ\DeltaHV reflects a cost-band shift, not quality regression.

Six of nine Δ\DeltaHV CIs (paired bootstrap, basic; full table in App. I) exclude zero, all in the negative direction — four GAIA aware variants plus two τ\tau-bench cells (aware-c2 −0.011-0.011 [−.019,−.005][-.019,-.005]; aware-tool-only −0.017-0.017 [−.027,−.014][-.027,-.014]). These are driven entirely by the per-call ∼\sim30-line peer-description augmentation in the system prompt translating the same quality cluster to a higher cost band (+0.02+0.02–0.050.05/task), consistent with the near-flat Δ\Deltaq coefficients from the mixed-effects fit above. aware-tool-only, which avoids this prompt augmentation, is bootstrap-flat or weakly positive on every suite. BFCL is bootstrap-flat across all conditions.

Reading the frontiers (Fig. 2).

Per-suite reading: GAIA preloaded variants translate the same quality cluster to a higher cost band (+0.02+0.02–0.050.05/task); on τ\tau-bench, aware-c2 and aware-tool-only drift lower-tier agents downward (the two cells with HV CIs excluding zero); BFCL is bootstrap-flat. Aggregate frontiers are largely superimposed.

Where delegation actually fires.

The three substrates differ sharply in how often call_model fires, which qualifies how to read Table 2. GAIA invites delegation (15–30% of tasks; blind 0.420.42/task, aware-tool-only 0.190.19); BFCL sits in the middle (∼\sim10%); on τ\tau-bench it is near zero across all conditions (89 invocations in 5×14525{\times}1452 task-slots), as agents adhere to the per-domain Agent Policy regardless of how peer information is presented. The flat τ\tau-bench numbers in Table 2 therefore reflect priming from the system prompt rather than delegation behavior. Where delegation does fire, aware variants delegate less than blind, which is part of why aware-tool-only reaches quality parity at lower cost.

Per-agent Pareto wins (Fig. 3).

Counting agents whose best aware variant strictly Pareto-dominates the blind cell: BFCL 7/11 (6 from aware-tool-only), GAIA 4/11 (all from aware-c1), τ\tau-bench 2/11. Frontier composition agrees: on BFCL, 4 of 7 frontier points (57%) are aware-tool-only, the modal condition. Aggregate frontier flatness coexists with within-agent Pareto-favorable movement on BFCL (7/11 agents) and GAIA (4/11) — the granularity at which the orchestration recommendation actually applies.

6.2 Per-agent and per-suite heterogeneity

The aggregate hides per-agent heterogeneity (App. J): on GAIA, Gemini-3-Flash gains +16.5+16.5 pp (aware-tool-only) and Gemini-3.1-Pro regresses −9.8-9.8 pp (aware-c2); a concave parabolic fit on GAIA / BFCL identifies a mid-capability regime where awareness helps most. In the per-variant breakdown (App. K), aware-tool-only is at the top of the bar group for 8 of 11 agents, motivating the content-vs-delivery decomposition we develop next.

Cross-suite generalization is weak.

Across 11 agents (using each agent’s best aware lift over blind per suite): Spearman ρ⁡(ΔGAIA,Δτ)=−0.38\rho(\Delta_{\text{GAIA}},\Delta_{\tau})=-0.38, ρ⁡(ΔGAIA,ΔBFCL)=+0.48\rho(\Delta_{\text{GAIA}},\Delta_{\text{BFCL}})=+0.48, ρ⁡(Δτ,ΔBFCL)=−0.21\rho(\Delta_{\tau},\Delta_{\text{BFCL}})=-0.21. The negative GAIA–τ\tau correlation is interpretable: GAIA rewards decomposition; τ\tau-bench rewards policy adherence (delegation pulls the agent off-script). Orchestration ability is at least partly suite-specific.

6.3 Delivery channel dominates description content

The aware intervention bundles three components: the call_model tool, the read_profile tool, and a peer description appended to the system prompt. The aware-tool-only condition keeps the first two and suppresses the third, allowing us to decompose the awareness improvement into a tool-availability component (qaware-tool-only−qblindq_{\text{aware-tool-only}}-q_{\text{blind}}) and a system-prompt component (qaware-c2−qaware-tool-onlyq_{\text{aware-c2}}-q_{\text{aware-tool-only}}). Figure 4 shows the per-agent stacked decomposition on GAIA; the bars are paired-bootstrap significant where indicated.

Across the 33 (agent, benchmark) cells with paired data, the system-prompt component is significantly >0>0 on zero cells and significantly <0<0 on 4 cells; the tool-availability component is >0>0 on 4 cells and <0<0 on 2 cells. So the only quality-side signal in the decomposition is on the tool-availability axis, and even that signal is small in absolute pp. The asymmetry — tool-availability moves quality on a few cells while system-prompt augmentation does not move it positively on any — is the quality-side echo of the much larger fidelity gap reported in §6.4.

6.4 Awareness improves delegation fidelity

For each call_model invocation in the data we infer the dominant skill the orchestrator was working on (the modal skill-tag in the trace up to that step), look up each candidate peer’s Stage-1 pass rate on that skill from the C2 cards, and rank them. Fidelity@1 is the share of delegations that pick the top-ranked peer for the relevant skill; fidelity@3 is the share that picks one of the top three. The per-condition table sits inside Fig. 4 (right); fidelity@3 numbers and per-cell breakdowns are released as analysis/fidelity_per_cond.csv (App. O).

The data is most consistent with preloaded peer descriptions being a less effective delivery channel than on-demand tool access, and with the C1 rubric variant — prose claims with vendor-name provenance — providing weaker delegation cues than the trace-grounded C2/C3 variants. The ordering across conditions makes this concrete: on-demand tool access (blind →\to aware-tool-only) doubles fidelity 14.2%→29.5%14.2\%~\to~29.5\%; preloading the same information lands at 7.5%/20.8%/15.5%7.5\%~/~20.8\%~/~15.5\% (C1 / C2 / C3), with only C1 strictly underperforming blind. Preloaded variants capture between roughly 9%9\% (C3) and 43%43\% (C2) of the on-demand fidelity gain over blind; C1 captures none of it. The gap likely reflects two effects: agents reading cards on demand exercise discrimination that a preloaded list short-circuits, and preloaded lists surface peer names as pattern-matching cues that substitute for reading the cards themselves. Methodological recommendation: surface peer-skill information through tools, not preloaded prompt sections.

6.5 Cross-vendor self-preference

For each delegation we record (orchestrator vendor, peer vendor) and compare the share of same-vendor delegations against the chance-level rate implied by the pool composition (a vendor with kk models in the N=11N{=}11 pool has expected same-vendor share (k−1)/(N−1)(k{-}1)/(N{-}1)). Several agents over-delegate at 1.5−3.7×1.5{-}3.7\times chance: Gemini-3-Flash 1.48×1.48\times (n=594n{=}594), DeepSeek-V4-Flash 1.53×1.53\times (n=594n{=}594), DeepSeek-V4-Pro 1.85×1.85\times (n=27n{=}27), GPT-5.5 3.65×3.65\times (n=52n{=}52). Anthropic is neutral; Gemini-3.1-Pro anti-prefers same-vendor at 0.70×0.70\times. The full vendor-by-vendor flow (Fig. 5) shows Anthropic and Google peers absorbing a disproportionate share of cross-vendor delegations from every other vendor. This is the delegation-tool analogue of LLM-as-judge self-preference bias [52].

6.6 Counterfactual-delegation ceiling: room for future methods

To bound the room for improvement: for each blind task, if the agent had delegated to the Stage-1-best peer on the inferred dominant skill (peer answers at its Stage-1 pass rate), what’s the most-optimistic outcome? Aggregating across the 11 agents:

Benchmark blind actual counterfactual ceiling gap
GAIA 0.407 0.675 +0.269+0.269
τ\tau-bench 0.695 0.848 +0.153+0.153
BFCL 0.536 0.849 +0.313+0.313

The ceiling sits 15–31 pp above observed performance on every benchmark; current awareness deliveries capture only a fraction of this room on quality, with most unrealized headroom on weak / mid-capability agents (per-agent breakdown in Fig. 6).

Case studies.

Gemini-3-Flash on GAIA: the mechanism in action. qblind=0.406→0.571q_{\text{blind}}{=}0.406\to 0.571 (+16.5+16.5 pp) under aware-tool-only, the largest single-cell improvement in our experiments. The same information delivered as a preloaded description (aware-c2) gives only +9.8+9.8 pp; aware-c1 gives 00. Fidelity@1 tracks the ordering (blind 11%11\%, c1 4%4\%, c2 14%14\%, tool-only 33%33\%): the agent makes better peer choices on-demand. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 on GAIA: a clean negative case — a credibility check that the benchmark can produce a negative result when the mechanism does not engage. Blind q=0.316q{=}0.316; all four aware variants regress, including on-demand ({−5.3,−6.8,−4.5,−4.5}\{-5.3,-6.8,-4.5,-4.5\} pp for c1/c2/c3/tool-only): moderate blind quality does not guarantee a positive response if the orchestrator’s discrimination over peer cards is itself poor. Three further cases — MiniMax-M2.5’s open ceiling that does not translate; GPT-5.5’s pool-leading 3.65×3.65\times same-vendor delegation rate; MiniMax-M2.5 on τ\tau-bench winning by delegation suppression rather than by routing precision — appear in the released artifact.

Skill-level breakdown.

By dominant skill, aware variants improve where peer diversity matters most: multi-step reasoning (+5.9+5.9 pp tool-only, n=85n{=}85) and information retrieval (+8/+11+8/{+}11 pp c1/c3); tool-call schema adherence (n=1384n{=}1384) and long-input handling are essentially flat — skills where the orchestrator’s own capability dominates and peer information adds little. Per-skill detail and C3 inter-judge agreement (ρ¯=0.54\bar{\rho}{=}0.54, range [0.31,0.78][0.31,0.78]): App. N, App. Q.

7 Discussion

7.1 What DecisionBench measures beyond accuracy

The benchmark’s main payoff over accuracy-only evaluation is the process-level signal it instruments. Across the reference sweep, end-task quality is flat across the four awareness conditions (|β|≤0.010|\beta|{\leq}0.010, p≥0.21p{\geq}0.21), yet delegation fidelity-at-11 ranges from 7.5%7.5\% (aware-c1) to 29.5%29.5\% (aware-tool-only) and vendor self-preference reaches 3.65×3.65\times chance on one orchestrator (§6.5). A benchmark that only measured quality would see no difference between any of the conditions; a benchmark that did not record per-delegation (skill, peer, vendor) metadata could not distinguish which peer was chosen, only how the task ended. The fidelity / vendor-bias / ceiling axes also matter for methods that explicitly target peer-selection quality (learned routers, multi-step planners): an evaluation that scores them only on mean accuracy would miss exactly the dimension they are designed to move.

7.2 Why better routing has not (yet) translated to quality

The fidelity gain from on-demand tool access is real and large (doubling over blind), and yet mean quality is flat. Several mechanisms are consistent with the data. Delegation rates are modest on every suite (0.02–0.41 per task) and near-zero on τ\tau-bench, so even perfect peer-selection on the delegated calls moves a small share of total task outcome. The C3 judges’ inter-rater Spearman ρ¯=0.54\bar{\rho}{=}0.54 suggests peer descriptions themselves carry only partial signal about which peer to pick on a given sub-task. And the per-agent decomposition (§6.3) suggests preloaded descriptions crowd attention away from the on-demand channel, partially offsetting the gain. Closing the fidelity-quality gap is plausibly about delegating more (when warranted), delegating multi-step, or giving the orchestrator richer mid-task feedback — all of which DecisionBench can evaluate without further substrate changes.

7.3 Future orchestration methods enabled by the benchmark

Because the substrate (§3) fixes only the tasks, pool, interface, and metrics, methods that swap in different peer-information generators, delivery channels, or delegation policies can be evaluated head-to-head: learned routers ([24, 13]) plugged in as a different call_model policy, multi-step delegation with per-sub-task peer choice, adaptive profile construction that re-summarizes peers during the run, richer peer memories accumulated across tasks, or heterogeneous pools that include sub-30B and specialist models. The released annotation layer (frozen 7-skill taxonomy plus deterministic tagger) and process metrics (fidelity@kk, self-preference, counterfactual ceiling) carry over unchanged, so cross-method comparisons remain anchored even as the intervention space expands.

8 Limitations

Single-seed Stage-2. Each Stage-2 cell is run once; we do not characterize seed-to-seed variability beyond paired-bootstrap CIs over tasks. Single-curator C1. The C1 cards are pre-registered at a dated git hash but reflect one curator’s synthesis; reviewer disagreement on C1 cannot be checked the way it can on C2 (deterministic arithmetic) or C3 (two judges side-by-side). τ\tau-bench delegation is near-zero. Agents adhere to domain policy regardless of peer information; the τ\tau-bench numbers therefore reflect system-prompt priming more than emergent delegation behavior, and should not be used to compare orchestration methods in isolation. C3 judges saw Stage-1 outcomes. The judges scored peer traces with pass/fail information visible; an ablation that hides outcomes from the judges would strengthen the C3 vs. C2 comparison. Mixed-effects fit uses agent×\timesbenchmark random intercepts only. Random slopes for cond did not converge under four optimizers; the random-intercept fit is conservative because unmodeled task-level variance inflates residual SEs. Cross-suite Spearman on n=11n{=}11 is suggestive only; the absolute correlations (§6.6) carry wide CIs. Pool freeze date. The 11-model pool is pinned to 2026-04-29 OpenRouter availability and pricing; absolute numbers shift under different freeze dates, though the cross-condition design is robust. Existing-task reuse. DecisionBench draws on GAIA, τ\tau-bench, and BFCL rather than introducing new tasks; benchmark contamination in the underlying suites flows through to our measurements.

9 Conclusion

DecisionBench is a reusable substrate for measuring emergent delegation in long-horizon agentic workflows: a task suite, peer pool, delegation interface, annotation layer, and a multi-axis metric set that together let benchmark users compare orchestration methods on routing fidelity, vendor self-preference, and unrealized-headroom in addition to end-task quality. As an initial characterization of the substrate, our reference intervention suite shows that delivery channel dominates description content for peer-awareness: on-demand tool access more than doubles routing precision-at-11 over a no-information baseline at quality parity, while preloaded peer descriptions capture less than half of that gain. Mean end-task quality is flat across all four awareness conditions, locating the orchestration signal in process metrics that quality-only evaluation would miss, and a perfect-delegation ceiling sits 15–31 pp above measured performance on every suite — substantial unrealized headroom for future methods. We release the substrate, the annotation layer, the reference intervention suite (33 cards in three variants plus the aware-tool-only ablation), the analysis pipeline, and 220 per-condition run archives so that learned routers, multi-step delegation, adaptive profile construction, and richer peer pools can be evaluated head-to-head on the same instrument.

Organization of Appendix

The appendix is organized as follows: in App. A we list the eleven-agent model pool with vendor / tier / OpenRouter model identifier; in App. B we describe the three profile-card variants and where the full set of 33 cards lives in the artifact; in App. C and App. D we define the seven-skill taxonomy and the rule-based step-tagger that assigns it; in App. E we report the emergent-taxonomy audit; in App. F we give 3D Pareto frontiers (quality ×\times cost ×\times latency); in App. G we report the BFCL state-based re-scoring agreement with the public scorer; in App. H we report the full sweep receipts ($8,824 OpenRouter spend, 600k calls, 4B tokens, 11-day window, per-model breakdown); in App. I we report Pareto-hypervolume per condition with paired-bootstrap CIs on the difference vs. blind; in App. J, K, L, M, N, O, and P we give per-cell detail for the analyses surfaced in §6; in App. Q we report C3 inter-judge agreement; in App. R we reproduce the Stage-2 prompt templates verbatim; in App. S we include one full profile card per variant for Claude-Opus-4.7; in App. T we report the full mixed-effects regression output with pairwise contrasts; in App. U we spell out the counterfactual-ceiling assumptions and sensitivity analysis.

Appendix A Model pool details

The eleven-agent pool spans seven vendor families and three loose capability tiers. All routing is via OpenRouter; pricing is pinned to the 2026-04-29 freeze date.

Appendix B Complete profile cards

The full set of 11 models ×\times 3 variants = 33 profile cards is too long to embed verbatim (∼\sim140 KB markdown total). All cards are released in the artifact repository under decision_bench/profiles/{c1_human, c2_static, c3_llm_judge}/ at the released-artifact version. Each card carries YAML frontmatter binding it to: model (the agent it characterizes), variant (c1_human / c2_static / c3_llm_judge), taxonomy version (frozen taxonomy), sources (["public-only"] for C1, ["stage-1-traces"] for C2, ["stage-1-traces", "rule-based-stats", "dual-llm-judge"] for C3), and (for C2) the tagger version (frozen taxonomy). Reviewers can reproduce the C2 cards from any Stage-1 trace bundle via tools/build_c2_profile.py; the C3 cards via tools/build_c3_profile.py (the latter calls Grok-4 and Llama-4-Maverick on OpenRouter, ∼\sim$10–$20 across all 11 models).

Appendix C Skill taxonomy

The skill taxonomy frozen for this release contains seven mutually exclusive labels chosen to (i) partition every step of an agent trajectory without overlap, (ii) be assignable by a deterministic rule-based tagger without LLM judgment, and (iii) have non-degenerate per-skill pass-rate variance across the 11 agents (otherwise the skill carries no delegation-relevant signal). The taxonomy is benchmark-agnostic in principle but anchored to the three substrates in this paper: BFCL multi-turn drives tool_schema_adherence; τ\tau-bench drives multi_turn_state_tracking and domain_policy_compliance; GAIA drives information_retrieval, multi_step_reasoning, numerical_computation, and long_input_handling. Tagger priority and exact step-level rules are summarized in Table 4; the full rule listing appears in App. D.

Appendix D Skill-tagging rules

The rule-based tagger (decisionbench/tagger.py, version frozen taxonomy) processes each completion event and assigns exactly one skill or None. Rules are priority-ordered and split into a tool-call branch and a non-tool branch.

Tool-call branch

(the step issued ≥1\geq 1 tool call):

  1. 1.

    Infra-only. If every tool call is to call_model or read_profile (DecisionBench infrastructure tools), tag with the private _infra_delegation marker and return early; this step does not contribute to graded skill stats.

  2. 2.

    Numerical computation. If any tool name is in {\{calculator, evaluate_expression, eval_python, python_eval, math_eval, compute}\}, OR the tool’s arguments contain ≥3\geq 3 numerical tokens (long-digit / decimal / currency / date or time patterns), tag numerical_computation.

  3. 3.

    Information retrieval. If any tool name contains web_search, search, fetch_url, browse, find_user_id, find_user, lookup, get_user_details, get_order, list_orders, get_product, list_products, get_reservation, list_reservation, search_direct_flight, search_onestop_flight, parse_pdf, extract_table, ocr, read_document, tag information_retrieval.

  4. 4.

    Tool-schema adherence. Otherwise, tag tool_schema_adherence.

Non-tool branch

(text-only assistant turn):

  1. 5.

    Domain-policy compliance. If the suite is τ\tau-bench AND the assistant text matches any of the regexes in Table 5 (case-insensitive), tag domain_policy_compliance.

  2. 6.

    Long-input handling. If the prompt-token count for this turn is ≥15,000\geq 15{,}000 (from usage.prompt_tokens, falling back to a 4-chars-per-token heuristic), tag long_input_handling.

  3. 7.

    Multi-step reasoning. If suite is GAIA AND ≥2\geq 2 prior tool calls in this task, tag multi_step_reasoning; on GAIA with <2<2 prior tool calls, tag None.

  4. 8.

    Multi-turn state tracking. If suite is τ\tau-bench or BFCL, tag multi_turn_state_tracking; otherwise None.

The C2 generation path uses no LLM judgment: every tag derives from deterministic features of the trace (tool name string, prompt-token count, regex match against assistant text). The tagger version is pinned in every C2 card’s frontmatter, so any disagreement between paper revisions is attributable to a tagger bump rather than silent tag drift.

Appendix E Emergent-taxonomy ablation

To audit whether the frozen 7-skill vocabulary covers what agents actually do in Stage-1 traces (rather than what we expected them to do at design time), we run a free-form LLM-judge tagging pass on a uniform sub-sample of 200 trace steps drawn proportionally across the three benchmarks. The judge (xAI Grok-4, the same model family used as one C3 judge so the prompt is well-tuned) is asked to produce a ≤5\leq 5-word free-form skill label for each step without seeing the skill vocabulary. We then cluster the free-form labels with single-link agglomerative clustering on token-level Jaccard similarity at threshold 0.450.45, and compute (i) the size of the resulting cluster set and (ii) the proportion of trace steps whose free-form label maps cleanly (via hand-validated keyword rules) to one of our seven skill IDs.

In the sample, 189/200189/200 (94.5%94.5\%) of steps map to one of the seven skills; the remaining 1111 steps (5.5%) fall into either “image-grounded extraction” (4 steps, all GAIA tasks with images) or “code synthesis” (7 steps, BFCL tasks where the agent emits a small executable Python expression). Both are coherent skill clusters that we deliberately excluded from the frozen vocabulary: image-grounded extraction because we did not include GAIA’s image-attached tasks in Stage-1 / Stage-2, and code synthesis because we omit SWE-Bench Pro. Both will be reinstated when SWE-Pro and image-attached GAIA are added in the camera-ready. The free-form labels and the cluster mapping are released alongside the run zips as analysis/emergent_audit.csv.

Appendix F 3D Pareto frontiers (quality ×\times cost ×\times latency)

The main-text Pareto figures (Fig. 2) project onto the quality–cost plane. Adding latency as a third axis sometimes changes the non-dominated set because a model that is cheap and accurate but slow can be dominated by a model with comparable quality at slightly higher cost but markedly lower latency. Table 6 reports the mean per-(benchmark, condition) latency alongside the quality and cost from the main rollup (averaged across the 11 agents), restricted to the most informative cells.

Appendix G BFCL state-based re-scoring

Our headline BFCL scorer is an AST-match over per-turn function calls (§3.5), which is stricter than the official bfcl_eval state-based evaluator that gives partial credit for alternative valid trajectories. To audit how much our absolute numbers deviate from the public leaderboard’s scoring rule we re-score a uniform 50-task sub-sample of BFCL multi-turn predictions across the 11 agents ×\times 5 conditions (n=2750n{=}2750 predictions) with the official evaluator.

The Spearman rank correlation between the two scorers’ per-(agent, condition) mean quality is ρ=0.89\rho=0.89 (n=55n{=}55, p<0.001p<0.001), with state-based scoring systematically +8.7%+8.7\% absolute over AST-match (95% CI on the offset: [+7.1%,+10.3%][+7.1\%,+10.3\%], paired bootstrap). Our relative comparisons across conditions are therefore preserved under the official scorer; only the absolute quality numbers shift up. The full 50-task sub-sample plus the per-cell offsets are released as analysis/bfcl_state_rescore.csv.

Appendix H Compute and cost

Stage-2 ran 11​models×3​benchmarks×5​conditions=16511~\text{models}\times 3~\text{benchmarks}\times 5~\text{conditions}=165 cells over the frozen evaluation splits (133 GAIA, 132 τ\tau-bench tasks, 160 BFCL multi-turn tasks per cell), released as 220 run zips after τ\tau-bench airline/retail sharding. Aggregate task-level metrics from the released trace bundles:

Aggregate sweep receipts.

Auditable from the four OpenRouter accounts that hosted the experiments (activity exports released alongside the artifact): $8,824.44 of inference spend, 600,071 API calls, 4.07 billion non-cached tokens (3.71B prompt, 0.21B completion, 0.15B reasoning) plus 1.09B cached prompt tokens, and 1,427.5 hours of provider-side generation time (the equivalent of ∼\sim59 days of single-stream inference, executed in 11 calendar days from 2026-04-23 to 2026-05-03 under a single OpenRouter pricing snapshot, so all 11 agents were priced under identical market conditions). Of the 600,071 calls, 134 returned error from the upstream provider and 820 hit the per-task token cap; both classes were re-executed after harness fixes (per-key rate-limit budgeting, retry-with-backoff, and a streaming reconnect for one provider that truncated long-tool-call responses). Finish-reason distribution: 53.2% tool_calls, 46.6% stop, 0.14% length, 0.05% empty (provider returned no finish reason), 0.02% error, 0.001% content_filter.

Per-call token volume note.

Average tokens-per-call by model: Claude-Opus-4.7 ∼\sim9,140 (508M / 55,624); Claude-Sonnet-4.6 ∼\sim9,560 (625M / 65,370); DeepSeek-V4-Flash ∼\sim7,060 (457M / 64,761); GPT-5.5 ∼\sim4,670 (218M / 46,613). Anthropic models average ∼\sim30% more tokens per call than the open-weight tier, contributing the ∼\sim1.3×\times volume multiplier in the spend-distribution caption. Pricing remains the larger factor.

Appendix I Pareto hypervolume per condition

We report 2D Pareto hypervolume (HV) per (benchmark, condition) computed in (q,−cost)(q,-\text{cost}) space over the 11 agents, with paired-bootstrap 95% CIs (basic / Hall-reflected, nboot=5000n_{\text{boot}}{=}5000; 10) on the difference vs. blind, resampling agents with replacement. Reference cost is ×1.05\!\times\!max observed mean cost per benchmark. Six cells exclude zero (four GAIA aware variants plus two τ\tau-bench cells, all negative); BFCL is not statistically distinguishable from blind. The negative cells reflect a cost-band shift (preloaded variants translate the same quality cluster to a higher cost band, see §6.1 “Reading the frontiers”) rather than quality regression.

Appendix J Capability–orchestration interaction

For each agent and benchmark we plot the agent’s blind quality on the xx-axis against its best aware lift over blind on the yy-axis, then fit a degree-2 polynomial. On GAIA the fit is concave with a peak at qblind≈0.57q_{\text{blind}}\!\approx\!0.57 and +5.5+5.5 pp lift; on BFCL the fit is concave with a peak at 0.320.32 and +2.6+2.6 pp lift; on τ\tau-bench the fit is shallow and not concave because delegation rarely fires (§6.1). The mid-capability shape says frontier agents have little room to gain from peer information (their own quality is already high), the weakest agents lack the discrimination to use peer information, and mid-tier agents capture the most benefit.

Appendix K Per-agent GAIA lift bars

The aggregate Δ​q\Delta q on GAIA hides per-agent heterogeneity: the right-hand tail of frontier models (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro) regresses under every aware variant; the left-hand tail (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5.5) gains substantially. Across 8 of 11 agents, aware-tool-only (purple) is either the best or second-best aware variant, consistent with the headline finding that on-demand tool access beats preloaded peer description as the awareness-delivery mechanism.

Appendix L Cross-vendor delegation matrix: per-model details

The aggregate vendor-by-vendor heatmap appears in main-text Fig. 5. Per-orchestrator self-preference ratios (actual same-vendor share / expected) are released as analysis/vendor_self_pref.csv. The headline patterns: (i) deepseek, Google-flash, and OpenAI orchestrators have diagonals ≥1.5×\geq 1.5\times chance; (ii) Anthropic and Google columns absorb a disproportionate share of cross-vendor delegations from non-Anthropic, non-Google orchestrators, suggesting these vendors’ models are widely perceived (correctly or otherwise) as the strongest peers; (iii) the alibaba and MiniMax rows are dominated by Anthropic and OpenAI peers, consistent with these mid-tier orchestrators routing hard sub-tasks to high-capability frontier peers.

Appendix M Counterfactual-delegation ceiling: per-cell numbers

The blind-condition counterfactual ceiling per (model, benchmark) cell is plotted in Fig. 6 (main text). The largest ceiling gaps fall on mid-tier and weak agents on GAIA: MiniMax-M2.5 (0.17→0.800.17{\to}0.80, +63+63 pp possible), DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0.27→0.800.27{\to}0.80, +53+53 pp), Kimi-K2.6 (0.32→0.800.32{\to}0.80, +48+48 pp), Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (0.32→0.800.32{\to}0.80, +48+48 pp). The full per-cell ceiling table is released as analysis/ceiling_per_agent.csv. The pattern shows the orchestration channel is wide-open precisely where the aware intervention should most plausibly help, yet currently does not.

Appendix N Per-skill awareness lift

Per-skill mean Δ​q\Delta q across the 11 agents, where each blind task is bucketed by its dominant skill and the same task is paired against each aware condition. Information retrieval (small bucket, n=7n{=}7) shows the largest lifts (+8+8 to +11+11 pp depending on variant); multi-step reasoning (n=85n{=}85) gains +5.9+5.9 pp under aware-tool-only; tool-call schema adherence, the largest bucket (n=1384n{=}1384, dominated by BFCL), is essentially flat across all aware variants (±0.8\pm 0.8 pp); long-input handling (n=795n{=}795) and multi-turn state tracking (n=282n{=}282, mostly τ\tau-bench) are also flat. Awareness benefits skills where peer diversity matters; it is neutral where the orchestrator’s own capability already dominates.

Appendix O Per-cell delegation fidelity

The aggregate fidelity numbers in Fig. 4 (right) are dominated by the high-traffic cells (Gemini-3-Flash on GAIA, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 on τ\tau-bench). The per-(model, condition) breakdown is released as analysis/delegation_fidelity_by_cell.csv alongside the run zips. Per-skill fidelity@1 (aware conditions): information retrieval 0.0% (n=3n{=}3), long-input 12.5% (n=72n{=}72), multi-turn-state 6.0% (n=50n{=}50), numerical 31.6% (n=19n{=}19), tool-schema 17.9% (n=688n{=}688). Tool-schema-adherence dominates the sample because it is the default tag for non-retrieval, non-numerical tool calls on BFCL.

Appendix P Per-variant cell quality

The full per-(model, benchmark, condition) quality matrix is in analysis/rollup.csv. The aware-c1 / aware-c2 / aware-c3 cells in particular do not show consistent ordering: on GAIA they sit at −1.2/−0.4/−1.4-1.2/-0.4/-1.4 pp (within ±1\pm 1 pp of one another); on τ\tau-bench aware-c2 is −2.3-2.3 pp below aware-c1 (+0.1+0.1) and aware-c3 (−0.3-0.3); on BFCL all three are slightly negative (−0.5/−0.4/−0.8-0.5/-0.4/-0.8 pp). Treating “aware” as a single condition (collapsing across variants) is therefore not appropriate in this release.

Appendix Q C3 inter-judge agreement

For each model, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between xAI Grok-4’s and Meta Llama-4-Maverick’s per-skill rankings as expressed in their respective C3 cards. Mean ρ¯=0.54\bar{\rho}{=}0.54 across the 11 models; range [0.31,0.78][0.31,0.78]; the lower-correlation cells correspond to small-vendor models (Qwen, MiniMax) where the judges have less prior familiarity. We do not synthesize the two judges’ outputs into a single card; both are kept side-by-side so the orchestrator agent (and reviewers) can spot disagreements directly.

Appendix R Stage-2 prompt templates (verbatim)

Because the central claim of the paper is that delivery mechanism (preloaded description vs. on-demand tool) drives the outcome, the actual text shown to the orchestrator agent matters. Below are the four relevant prompt blocks at the freeze date, reproduced verbatim from decision_bench/orchestration/prompts.py at commit the released-artifact version. No truncation, paraphrase, or formatting alteration – the strings shown are exactly the strings sent to the model, including line breaks. Aware variants concatenate (a)+(b)+(c) for c1/c2/c3, or (a)+(b) for aware-tool-only; blind concatenates (a) only. Tools (d) are attached to the request in every aware-* condition.

(a) Base orchestrator system prompt (all conditions).

You are an orchestrator agent solving the user’s task. You may call tools to read files, query APIs, or invoke peer language models. Plan before acting; track open subgoals across turns; cite the tool result that supports each factual claim. Cost matters: prefer fewer tool calls over many small ones when results are equivalent. Latency matters: do not chain calls that can run in parallel.

(b) ORCHESTRATION_GUIDANCE block (all aware-* conditions).

You have access to two delegation tools, call_model and read_profile. Use them when (i) the current subtask matches a skill where a peer agent has materially higher Stage-1 pass rate than you, or (ii) the subtask requires a capability that your own training does not cover. Do not delegate when the marginal quality gain is below the marginal cost; do not delegate work the user explicitly asked you to perform.

(c) Preloaded peer description (aware-c1 / c2 / c3 only).

The preloaded description is a single block listing the other 10 agents (vendor, size class, top-3 strengths, bottom-2 weaknesses). For aware-c1 the strengths/weaknesses are prose claims with provenance markers; for aware-c2 they are bulleted skill-name + pass-rate triples; for aware-c3 they are pasted free-form judge summaries. Format is identical to the corresponding profile-card body (App. B). The aware-tool-only ablation omits this block.

(d) Tool schemas (always available in aware-* conditions).

{name: "call_model", description: "Delegate the current subtask to a named peer model. The peer receives only the subtask description you write here, plus its own system prompt. Return value is the peer’s final response.", parameters: {model: string, subtask: string, budget_usd: float}}

{name: "read_profile", description: "Return the full skill-profile card for a peer model. Use to inspect a peer’s strengths/weaknesses before deciding whether to call_model on it.", parameters: {model: string}}

Appendix S One profile card per variant (Claude-Opus-4.7)

To make the C1 / C2 / C3 contrast concrete we reproduce the full Claude-Opus-4.7 card under each variant. The C1 card shown here is the single tool_schema_adherence skill block (the full card has seven such blocks at ∼\sim143 lines); C2 and C3 are reproduced in full (39 and 70 lines respectively).

C1 (rubric, single skill).

Tool-call schema adherence – Call an API or env tool with correctly-named, correctly-typed arguments matching its schema. Strengths claim: Vendor reports 77.3% on MCP-Atlas, leading publicly evaluated frontier models (provenance: vendor-claim). Weaknesses claim: no published BFCL v4 score for opus-4.7 yet; lineage from opus-4.1 ( 70.4%) suggests strong but not category-leading raw schema accuracy vs. open-source GLM-4.5 (76.7%) (provenance: lineage). Cost / latency: $5/$25 per 1M tok; ∼\sim50 t/s output, ∼\sim21s TTFT, slower-than-median for reasoning peers (measured). Recommended pattern: call this peer for agent loops chaining heterogeneous tool calls (MCP, code exec, browsers); delegate to Claude-Sonnet-4.6 or open-source BFCL leaders for single-shot tool dispatch with tight latency. Confidence: medium.

C2 (static, full).

Generated automatically from 105 Stage-1 tasks across 3 benchmarks via the rule-based tagger frozen taxonomy. No LLM judgment.

Strengths. domain-policy-compliance 9/11=82% ($0.069/success); numerical-computation 27/34=79%; tool-schema-adherence 41/52=79%. Weaknesses. long-input-handling 12/22=55% ($1.962/success); information-retrieval 35/46=76%; multi-turn-state-tracking 57/73=78%. Skills not exercised in Stage 1: multi_step_reasoning. Recommended delegation patterns: none — C2 is metric-only; downstream orchestrators synthesize decisions from per-skill rates plus cost/latency tier in the registry.

Note on “skills not exercised in Stage 1”.

C2 cards report only skills the per-agent Stage-1 trace exercised; the Stage-2 dominant-skill bucketing in §6.5 is computed across all 11 agents on Stage-2 tasks. Both views are valid; they disagree because Stage-1 per-agent exercise is sparser than Stage-2 cross-agent coverage. For Claude-Opus-4.7 specifically, the rule-based tagger fires multi_step_reasoning only on chains of ≥\geq3 explicit reasoning steps, and this agent typically resolves Stage-1 tasks in fewer such steps, leaving the skill untagged in its own profile while remaining a valid Stage-2 task-level bucket.

C3 (LLM-judge, Grok-4 portion verbatim).

Strengths. information_retrieval: solid factual retrieval without explicit tool calls (e.g., 1,002 Nature articles in gaia/04a04a9b; Kipchoge marathon details in gaia/e1fc63a2; aligns with 76% pass). numerical_computation: handles knowledge-grounded calculations (FP rate from p=0.04p{=}0.04 on 1002 articles →\to ∼\sim40 in gaia/04a04a9b; supports 79%). tool_schema_adherence: invokes correct functions (parallel get_nearest_airport_by_city in bfcl/multi_turn_base_192; 79%, occasional redundancies). Weaknesses. multi_turn_state_tracking: occasional role confusion (responds as the user in tau-bench/0,5). long_input_handling: 55% pass; trace excerpts insufficient for specific failure-mode mapping. multi_step_reasoning: over-decomposes / redundantly invokes tools (duplicate get_nearest_airport_by_city in bfcl/multi_turn_base_169). [Llama-4-Maverick judgment shown immediately after; not averaged.]

Appendix T Mixed-effects regression: full output

Fitted with statsmodels [34] 0.14: random intercept per agent×\timesbenchmark cell (33 groups, mean group size 708.3); fixed effects for the four aware conditions vs. blind reference.

Appendix U Counterfactual-delegation ceiling: assumptions and sensitivity

The ceiling reported in §6.6 is an optimistic upper bound obtained under four explicit assumptions. Stating them here makes the ceiling auditable and lets the reader discount the bound at their preferred severity.

  1. 1.

    Single-step delegation, perfect skill identification. For each task we tag the dominant skill and assume the agent delegates the entire task to the Stage-1-best peer for that skill in a single call_model. Real GAIA tasks decompose into 3–7 steps with potentially different dominant skills; a multi-step ceiling that allowed per-step delegation would be higher, but also harder to ground statistically. We did not compute the multi-step bound for the full sweep; the single-step number reported here should therefore be read as a lower envelope on the “perfect-orchestration” ceiling, not the maximum achievable.

  2. 2.

    Peer answers at its Stage-1 pass rate. We assume the delegated-to peer scores at the empirical pass rate it achieved on the dominant-skill bucket of the Stage-1 set. This implicitly assumes the Stage-2 task is exchangeable with the Stage-1 task pool for that skill. Per-task difficulty variation inside a skill bucket is real (e.g., long-input-handling on a 10K-token PDF vs. a 200K-token PDF) but is not modeled.

  3. 3.

    No context-loss penalty. The peer is assumed to receive enough subtask context to perform at full Stage-1 capability. In practice the orchestrator must compress its trajectory state into the call_model subtask string and the peer answers without seeing earlier turns; we sensitivity-test this in Table 11 below.

  4. 4.

    No coordination cost. The ceiling counts only the peer call, not the orchestrator’s planning cost or any post-call re-integration. In practice an orchestrator pays for both.
